newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban dissidents attack Communist Party document.
newsitem.headline: Cuban dissidents attack Communist Party document.

text.p: A group of dissidents on Friday accused Cuba's ruling Communist Party of wanting to maintain "totalitarian control" over the island while failing to solve its economic problems and called for free elections.

The Working Group of Internal Dissidence, made up of four dissidents who say they have the support of 14 other small groups, called a news conference for foreign correspondents in the cramped living room of one of the group's members, Martha Beatriz Roque, to criticise a document prepared by the Communist Party for its Fifth Congress in October.

"The philosophy of the government is not to serve the people but to be its dictator," the dissidents charged in a counter-document that said the ruling party had not guaranteed Cubans "a quality of life that has a decent minimum."
"Its policy pursues the objective of having power through totalitarian control," the dissident document said.

They were replying to a document issued last month by the Communist Party for discussion ahead of the October congress that will set party strategy for the coming years. The party document makes plain President Fidel Castro's government has no intention of changing the current one-party socialist system and believes Cubans must unite behind this concept.
"We cannot accept that a government that has dedicated itself to dividing the country can talk in the name of unity," the dissident paper said.

The Communist Party document, currently being debated across the island of 11 million people at meetings called by party branches and mass organisations such as neighbourhood watch groups, draws on history since Cuba's 19th century struggle for independence from Spain to argue that the current system is the only alternative.

It presents the United States as a constant danger to Cuba's independence and says the one-party system and the unity of Cubans is the only defence. Washington, which maintains a 35-year economic embargo against Cuba, is the most aggressive advocate of political change on the island that became a Soviet-backed society after Castro's 1959 revolution.

Cuba plunged into a severe economic crisis after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. The dissident paper criticised the party document for failing to offer solutions to Cuba's economic woes and called for free elections.

"If, as the leadership claims, most Cubans support the Communist Party, then there is no reason not to call free elections, under international supervision, which would silence all detractors of the system," the dissidents said.
The "Working Group," composed of dissidents Roque, Rene Gomez Manzano, Vladimiro Roca and Felix Bonne Carcasses, said it was attempting to unify Cuba's fragmented opposition.

Cuba's scattered dissident groups are small and illegal and their members are subject to official harassment and sometimes detention or prison terms. Authorities call them groups "grupusculos," tiny bodies with no significance, and say they are puppets of a U.S. policy seeking to destroy Cuba.

The groups have little room for action since they have no access to state-run media and cannot call public meetings. They are limited to expressing their views to foreign media, diplomats and occasional visitors from foreign governments.
Some of their opinions filter back to Cubans, mostly via Radio Marti, a U.S. government-funded anti-Castro radio station that is listened to by some citizens.
